---
title: "Discovering R Installations"
description: "Learn how Positron finds R installations on macOS, Windows, and Linux, and how to hide installations or set a default R for a folder."
---

This guide explains how Positron finds R installations. It also shows how to use settings to hide installations from the **Interpreter picker** and to choose which R starts in a folder. For using R in Positron, see our [R language guide](guide-r.qmd).

## R installation discovery

Positron consults various sources to build the list of available R interpreters:

* Well-known R root folders for the specific operating system:
  - macOS: `/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions`
  - Linux: `/opt/R`
  - Windows: `%ProgramW6432%/R` (typically resolves to `C:/Program Files/R`) and
    `%LOCALAPPDATA%/Programs/R` (typically resolves to
    `C:/Users/username/AppData/Local/Programs/R`)

  These locations are treated as so-called root folders, meaning we expect them
  to contain one or more versions of R, not to actually be an R installation.
* The R on your `PATH`, which is the R that `which R` finds. By default, Positron does not look here on Windows. To change this, set [`positron.r.interpreters.pathDiscoveryMode`](positron://settings/positron.r.interpreters.pathDiscoveryMode).
* Well-known paths to an R executable or to a symlink that resolves to an R executable, e.g.:
  - `/usr/bin/R`
  - `/usr/local/bin/R`
  - `/opt/local/bin/R`
  - `/opt/homebrew/bin/R`
* R installations recorded in the Windows registry, in keys such as:
  - `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\R-core\R64\X.Y.Z`
  - `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\R-core\R64\X.Y.Z`
  where `X.Y.Z` is a concrete R version, such as 4.4.2.
  - It's often possible to discover which of those R versions is considered
    the current version of R from the registry keys
    `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\R-core\R64\InstallPath` or
    `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\R-core\R64\InstallPath`.

## Customizing R discovery

Settings let you change where Positron looks for R, which R installations it shows, and which one it starts.
You can navigate to these settings by running the _Preferences: Open Settings_ command from the Command Palette.
Then select **Extensions > R > Advanced**.

You typically need to use absolute paths in these settings and not rely on shell features, such as parameter expansion (e.g., `${HOME}`). However, these settings do support the `${workspaceFolder}` variable.
The settings [`positron.r.customRootFolders`](positron://settings/positron.r.customRootFolders), [`positron.r.customBinaries`](positron://settings/positron.r.customBinaries), and the [`positron.r.interpreters.exclude`](positron://settings/positron.r.interpreters.exclude), [`positron.r.interpreters.override`](positron://settings/positron.r.interpreters.override), and [`positron.r.interpreters.default`](positron://settings/positron.r.interpreters.default) support this variable and you can use it to point Positron to an R installation inside your project:

```{.json filename="settings.json"}
{
  "positron.r.customBinaries": ["${workspaceFolder}/.pixi/envs/default/bin/R"]
}
```

Positron supports only the `${workspaceFolder}` variable in these settings.
In a multi-root workspace, it refers to the first folder.
Positron ignores a path that uses any other variable, such as `${env:NAME}`, or that uses `${workspaceFolder}` when no folder is open, and logs the reason.

To give an R installation its own label, environment variables, environment modules, or startup script, see [Interpreter definitions](interpreter-definitions.qmd).

### Finding R in other locations

If Positron does not find an R installation, use these settings to tell it where to look:

* [`positron.r.customRootFolders`](positron://settings/positron.r.customRootFolders): Suitable for R root folders that contain 1 or more R installations.
  - Hypothetical example: `C:/nonstandardRLocation`
* [`positron.r.customBinaries`](positron://settings/positron.r.customBinaries): Suitable for specific R executables.
  - Hypothetical example: `C:/nonstandardRLocation/R-4.4.1/bin/x64/R.exe`
* [`positron.r.interpreters.condaDiscovery`](positron://settings/positron.r.interpreters.condaDiscovery): Enables discovery of R installations managed by conda. This support is experimental and not all Positron features may work as expected.
* [`positron.r.interpreters.pixiDiscovery`](positron://settings/positron.r.interpreters.pixiDiscovery): Enables discovery of R installations managed by pixi. This support is also experimental.
* [`positron.r.interpreters.pathDiscoveryMode`](positron://settings/positron.r.interpreters.pathDiscoveryMode): Controls whether Positron looks for the R on your `PATH`, which is the R that `which R` finds.
  - `auto` (the default): Looks on macOS and Linux, but not on Windows, where searching the `PATH` can be slow.
  - `on`: Always looks.
  - `off`: Never looks.

### Hide or limit R installations

To keep Positron from using some R installations, use one of these settings.
Positron does not show these installations in any interpreter list, and it does not start them.

* [`positron.r.interpreters.exclude`](positron://settings/positron.r.interpreters.exclude): Hides specific R installations. Each path is an R executable or a folder. A folder hides every R installation at or under that folder. This also applies to R installations that Positron finds through `positron.r.customRootFolders` or `positron.r.customBinaries`.
  - Example: `/opt/R/4.2.3` hides R 4.2.3 on Linux.
* [`positron.r.interpreters.override`](positron://settings/positron.r.interpreters.override): Shows only specific R installations. Each path is an R executable or a folder of R installations. Do not use the folder of one installation, such as `/opt/R/4.4.2`, because Positron finds nothing there.
  - Example: `/opt/R` shows only the R installations in `/opt/R` on Linux.
  - Example: `/opt/R/4.4.2/bin/R` shows only R 4.4.2 on Linux.

When you set `override`, Positron does not search anywhere else.
It skips all of these sources:

* The locations at the top of this page
* The `PATH`
* The Windows registry
* The `r-versions` file that Posit Workbench and RStudio Server use
* R installations from conda, pixi, and environment modules
* The `positron.r.customRootFolders` and `positron.r.customBinaries` settings in [Finding R in other locations](#finding-r-in-other-locations)

When you set `override`, Positron ignores `exclude`. If both settings include the same R installation, Positron still shows it.

### Choose which R starts

[`positron.r.interpreters.default`](positron://settings/positron.r.interpreters.default) sets the R that Positron starts for the folder you have open, even if you used a different R in that folder last time.
This setting controls which R starts, not when R starts.
To control when R starts, use the [`interpreters.startupBehavior`](positron://settings/interpreters.startupBehavior) setting, described in [Interpreter Startup](interpreter-startup.qmd).

Set `positron.r.interpreters.default` to the path of one R executable.
The executable must exist on disk, and the path cannot point to a folder.

* Example on Linux: `/opt/R/4.4.2/bin/R`
* Example on macOS: `/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/4.4-arm64/Resources/bin/R`
* Example on Windows: `C:/Program Files/R/R-4.4.2/bin/x64/R.exe`

Where you set `positron.r.interpreters.default` decides which folders use it:

* In your user settings, the setting applies to every folder you open.
* In a project's `.vscode/settings.json` file, the setting applies only to that project's folder. If you set it in both places, Positron uses the project's value.

Positron ignores `positron.r.interpreters.default` in these cases:

* The path is in `exclude`, or is inside a folder in `exclude`.
* You set `override`, and the path is not in `override` or inside a folder in `override`.
* The path does not exist.

In these cases, Positron chooses an R as though you had not set `positron.r.interpreters.default`.

## Unsupported R installations

Positron only supports R 4.2 and higher.
Older R versions might be discovered in the search described above, but they will be discarded.

On macOS, Positron only supports the system's current R version and other R installations that are orthogonal.

What does orthogonal mean here?
The `R` executable on macOS (and Linux) is actually a shell script that's responsible for launching R.
In an orthogonal R installation, this script targets the home of a specific, concrete version of R, such as `/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/4.4-arm64`.
In a non-orthogonal R installation, this script targets the home of the current R version (literally, `/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Resources`, which is a symlink).
The CRAN installer leaves a non-orthogonal R installation behind and, by default, removes the previous version of R.

The notion of orthogonality comes from a tool called [rig: The R Installation Manager](https://github.com/r-lib/rig).
We highly recommend rig for managing R installation, especially for macOS users who want to have more than one functioning R installation.

## Troubleshooting

The discovery process is logged in the R Language Pack channel.
You can learn more in the [troubleshooting guide](troubleshooting.qmd).
